explanations.explanation: That's the spot, baker. David says, "I will walk in my house with integrity of heart." Anybody can look holy at a crowded event. Your own house is where nobody is clapping. I think David started there on purpose.

The city gates sound like a good guess, since that's where a king is out in public. But David says, "I will walk in my house with integrity of heart." He names his own home. I think that's the harder place to be consistent, because nobody's watching.
A battlefield would make for a loud, dramatic psalm, friend. But David says, "I will walk in my house with integrity of heart." His promise is about his own home, not a war. Quiet places count too.

explanations.answer: He hates it and it won't cling to him
explanations.explanation: Yep, baker. David says, "I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me." He's not just avoiding it, he says he hates it. And he says it shall not cling to him, so he wants none of it stuck on him.

explanations.answer: He'll study it so he can learn from it
explanations.explanation: Studying it sounds smart, baker, but that's not what David says. He says, "I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me." He doesn't plan to take notes on it. He wants it kept off him.

explanations.answer: He'll leave it for someone else to judge
explanations.explanation: Passing it along to somebody else would be easy, friend. But David says it himself: "I hate the work of those who fall away; it shall not cling to me." He takes a stand, and the stand is about what sticks to him.
That's it, baker. David says, "I will know nothing of evil." He's saying he won't get familiar with it. I think that's a pretty big promise to make out loud.
Sorrow is a natural thing to guess, friend. But David says, "I will know nothing of evil." He doesn't promise a life without sadness. His promise is about keeping evil out of his life.
Weakness is a fair guess, but it isn't in the verse. David says, "I will know nothing of evil." He doesn't brag about being strong. He says what he'll refuse to get to know.

Right on, baker. David says, "Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence…" Slander in secret is the kind that hides, and David says he'll shut it down. The verse gives no steps in between.

A warning feels fair, friend, but the verse doesn't mention one. David says, "Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence…" He doesn't spell out any steps before that. We only get what he says.
A fine is a reasonable guess, baker, but David says something else: "Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, I will put to silence…" No payment is mentioned. He says he'll silence them.

True, baker. David says, "the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure." Haughty eyes look down on other people, and a proud heart is that same pride on the inside. David names both together, and he says he won't put up with that person.

That one's true, friend. David says, "the one with haughty eyes and a proud heart, I will not endure." Haughty eyes look down on other people, and a proud heart is pride on the inside. He names both together and says he will not endure that person, so the statement isn't false.
That's right. David says, "My eyes favor the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me…" His eyes favor them. The faithful are the ones he says may dwell with him.

A king might be expected to want soldiers, baker. But David says, "My eyes favor the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me…" He says faithful, not mighty. The verse is about who they are, not how strong they are.

explanations.answer: The wise men of the east
explanations.explanation: Wise men from far away would make a fancy guest list, friend. But David says, "My eyes favor the faithful of the land, that they may dwell with me…" He's looking at the faithful in his own land. Faithful is the word he picks.

Yes, baker. David says, "he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me." Walking in integrity is what he's looking for in the people who serve him. Notice it's the same word, integrity, that he used for himself in verse 2 (Psalm 101:2).

Bowing is a fair guess, friend, but that's not the word. David says, "he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me." To minister is to serve, so the person walking in integrity is the one who serves him. The word is minister, not bow.

Singing fits the psalm, since David talks about singing in Psalm 101:1. But in this line he says, "he who walks in the way of integrity shall minister to me." The word is minister, baker. Good guess though.
Not quite, baker. David says, "No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house…" So the answer is no, deceit doesn't get a room. The verse closes that door.

That's right, friend. David says, "No one who practices deceit shall dwell in my house; no one who tells lies shall stand in my presence." So deceit doesn't get to move in. Lying doesn't get to stand in front of him either.

That's it, baker. David says, "Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land…" Every morning, not once in a while. I set my timer for a lot of things, but I'd have a hard time keeping up with this one.

A new moon only comes around once a month, friend, so that would be a slower schedule. David says, "Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land…" Morning means daily. That's a much busier plan.
Every Sabbath would be once a week, baker. But David says, "Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land…" Morning, every single time. He doesn't wait for a special day.

Not quite, friend. David does start in his own house (Psalm 101:2), but the last line goes wider. He says, "…that I may cut off every evildoer from the city of the LORD." The city is bigger than one house.

Right, baker. He starts with his house (Psalm 101:2), but the last verse reaches out. David says, "Every morning I will remove all the wicked of the land…" and "…every evildoer from the city of the LORD." The land and the city are a lot more than one house.
